name: Hair part theory

lead: Hair part theory says that where hair is divided on the scalp (centre, side, deep side or off-centre) shifts the visual balance of the face. Proponents say a part on the side that matches or offsets facial asymmetries makes the face look more symmetrical, and stylists link part choice to face shape.

It costs nothing to try and is reversible within minutes, which is much of its appeal. Stylists quoted in magazine guides give shape-based suggestions, while forum users describe preferring one side because it looks more symmetrical on them.

paras: People comb hair flat, try centre, side and off-centre parts in a mirror, and use the natural growth pattern or cowlick as a starting point. Stylists recommend experimenting. Styling products, cuts and bangs change how a part reads.
Minimal. Switching away from the natural part may need more styling effort, and tight or repeated parting in the same line can stress the hair in that spot.

web.title: InStyle on where to part your hair

chain: Choose centre, side or off-centre part
Hair frames brow and forehead differently
Face looks more balanced or symmetrical to the wearer
angle.text: A part can be changed at no cost and is visible in the mirror immediately. People use it to balance an uneven face, shorten or lengthen the look of the face, or hide a cowlick.

lead: Hair part theory is the proposition that the position and side of a hair part affect facial balance and perceived symmetry, so that choosing the right parting is a low-cost way to improve appearance. It appears on looksmaxxing forums as a small framing and styling detail alongside haircut and face-shape discussions.

The chain: a part sets how hair frames the forehead and brow, which changes how long, wide or even the face appears, which stylists and forum users use to pick a flattering look. Magazine stylists give common rules: centre parts suit symmetrical faces and can make shorter, wider faces look longer, side parts are versatile, and off-centre parts draw less attention to unevenness [1].
A medical-hypotheses paper has proposed factors that influence where people position the parting line [2]; beyond that, the theory rests on stylist experience and personal preference.
infobox: Centre, side, deep side, diagonal, off-centre

paras: Parting is the line along which hair is divided on the scalp. The theory holds that its position matters for facial harmony, a view expressed both by stylists and by forum members who describe choosing a side because it looks "more symmetrical" with their face [3].

In a 2017 InStyle guide, celebrity stylist Cheryl Bergamy said a centre part can balance forehead and chin on a heart-shaped face, and colorist Silvia Reis described it as the least forgiving if there are uneven areas on the face [1]. Side parts were described as suiting nearly any face shape, and deep side or diagonal parts as dramatic or softer alternatives. An off-centre part was suggested as often the best choice for a front cowlick, and Reis advised experimenting since parts are easy to change [1].

Medical research on hair parting mostly concerns the scalp: dermatologists assess central parting width to grade female pattern hair loss using the Sinclair scale [4]. A paper in Medical Hypotheses proposed explanations for preferences in positioning the parting line [2]. No study cited here has tested whether part position changes perceived facial attractiveness.
No studies found on hair part position and facial attractiveness. Related clinical work uses the width of the central part to score female pattern hair loss [4].
Forum threads discuss which side to part and whether a given side looks more symmetrical, with users reporting personal preferences despite natural growth patterns [3].

lore.intro: Members discuss parting side as a symmetry adjustment [3].
